I retain these wholly original XML fixtures to test the actual CodeWalker XML dialect. Codex generated their geometry and placement data through the pinned public CodeWalker APIs, then called the real XML exporter. They contain no installed GTA building or extracted proprietary resource.

The nine groups contain 27 XML resources. The empty-map group deliberately has no selectable building. The other 24 resources exercise ordinary placement, a wall and passage, closed boxes with eight noncoplanar vertices and twelve triangles each, stored quaternions, nonuniform scale, collision centres, composite transforms and packed material identities. A wider original collision variant changes only the collision resource while retaining the same placement and archetype metadata; this is a controlled invalidation input, not proof of a real archetype bounding box.

`reference.json` was generated by `tools/Test-CodeWalkerXmlReference05.ps1` and `tests/CodeWalkerXmlReference05.cs` using the independently built public CodeWalker profile at commit `485d56bec00262ed7fa472261cce7bbc6202b96e`. The oracle invokes the actual XML parser, resource rebuild, existing static DTO adapter, `YmapEntityDef` orientation/scale/position, `BoundGeometry.GetVertexPos` and SharpDX world transformation. Five hash vectors also retain CodeWalker's case-sensitive XML hash behavior, including the reserved `hash_1` spelling.

I compare semantic static fields and world vertices with explicit float tolerances. This establishes the supported XML algorithm on original inputs. It does not establish Enhanced installation provenance, a real entity-to-collision match, native metre calibration, activation state, acoustic material response, complete map coverage or genuine Los Santos compatibility.

The exporter emits error placeholders in some map sections not represented by the static subset. My decoder reports those sections as unknown; it does not treat them as decoded world geometry.
